choices.title: Bladder exstrophy
choices.correct_explanation:
The congenital anomaly seen in the above image is exstrophy of the bladder (ectopia vesicae).

Ectopia Vesicae

·         Bladder exstrophy refers to herniation of the urinary bladder through an anterior abdominal wall defect. The bladder is open and exposed on the outside of the abdomen. The male to female ratio is 4:1. Chronic exposure of the bladder to the external environment can lead to adenocarcinoma of the bladder.

·         It is associated with epispadias.        

·         The clinical features of bladder exstrophy include:

o   Separation of the pubic bones with non-united symphysis pubis

o   Epispadias

o   In males: Broad and short penis and bilateral inguinal hernia

o   In females: Bifid clitoris

·         Management involves a staged surgical reconstruction of the bladder and genitalia. Closure of the abdominal and bladder wall is done in the first year of life. This often requires an iliac osteotomy to relax the tension on the bladder and repair the abdominal wall during wound-healing.

·         Later, reconstruction of the bladder neck, sphincters, epispadias, and other genital defects is done.

Omphalocele   

·         Omphalocele refers to a congenital defect of the abdominal wall in which the bowel and solid viscera are covered by the peritoneum and amniotic membrane.

·         During normal development of the human embryo, the midgut herniates outward through the umbilical ring and continues to grow.       

·         Between 10th - 12th week of gestation, the midgut returns to the coelomic cavity and undergoes proper rotation and fixation, along with the closure of the umbilical ring.   

·         If the intestine fails to return, the infant is born with the abdominal contents protruding directly through the umbilical ring, with an intact sac covering the abdominal viscera, termed an Omphalocele.

·         The sac is composed of an outer layer of amnion and an inner layer of peritoneum. It is seen in Omphalocele and not in Gastroschisis. Omphalocele can vary from a small defect with intestinal contents to a giant omphalocele in which the abdominal wall defect measures 4 cm or more in diameter. It may even contain liver.    

Gastroschisis

·         Gastroschisis represents a congenital anomaly characterized by a defect in the anterior abdominal wall. The abdominal contents protrude through this defect. It is the most common anomaly seen in babies born to mothers under 20 years of age. Unlike omphalocele, there is no overlying sac and the size of the defect is usually <4 cm.  

·         An orogastric tube is placed to decompress the stomach. For primary closure, bowel loops are reduced, fascia and skin are approximated.    

·         If the viscera cannot be reduced into the abdomen, a silo is placed at the bedside. The eviscerated intestines are reduced serially during 5 to 7 days, followed by operative fascial closure.

choices.title: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
choices.correct_explanation:
• A woman presenting with persistent or rising β-hCG levels and abnormal uterine bleeding following evacuation of a molar pregnancy most likely has gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). This condition represents persistent trophoblastic disease that continues to proliferate after the molar tissue should have been removed.
  • Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) refers to the aggressive invasion of the endometrium and myometrium by trophoblast cells. It includes invasive mole, gestational choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumors, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors.
  • Malignant forms of GTO are termed gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN).

• Invasive mole (malignant)

• Choriocarcinoma (malignant)

• Placental site trophoblastic tumor (malignant)

• Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor (malignant)

GTN is diagnosed based on elevated β-hCG levels, FIGO criteria for diagnosis of GTN:

  • Persistence of β-hCG level plateau in 4 measurements for 3 weeks or longer
  • Rise in β-hCG levels in 3 or more consecutive measurements done weekly, over a period of 2 weeks or longer
  • Elevated β-hCG level for 6 months or more

After evacuation, persistence or spread of the disease is termed gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), not progressive mole. Hence, this term is outdated and incorrect in this context.

  • Option d: Ectopic pregnancy: Presents with lower abdominal pain, amenorrhea, and mild bleeding, often before 8 weeks’ gestation. β-hCG levels are usually lower than expected for gestational age and do not rise appropriately, rather than being markedly elevated.

choices.correct_explanation:
Nausea and vomiting are acute adverse effects of lithium therapy, and since lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, monitoring the lithium level immediately is the most appropriate action.

Lithium in Bipolar Disorder

·         Lithium is the drug of choice for maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder. It is also the most effective long-term treatment choice for bipolar disorder. Along with it, anticonvulsants and antipsychotics - e.g., olanzapine, and benzodiazepines are also used.

·         Lithium carbonate is the salt of monovalent cation lithium.  It is predominantly used to cure episodes of mania.

·         Indications: Mania, hypomania, bipolar disorder, etc.

·         Blood levels of lithium:

  • For therapeutic purpose (treatment of acute mania): 0.8-1.2 mEq/L
  • For prophylaxis (to prevent relapse of bipolar disorder): 0.5-0.8 mEq/L
  • Toxic levels of lithium: >/= 1.5 mEq/L

Note: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (0.8-1.2 mEq/L) and therefore requires monitoring to suspect toxicity. The toxic effects of lithium usually start manifesting when the serum level crosses 1.5 mEq/L.

Contraindications:

  • CKD
  • Heart disease
  • Hyponatremia or diuretic use

Baseline studies:

  • Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, calcium, and urine analysis
  • Thyroid function test
  • ECG in patients with coronary risk factors

Acute adverse effects:

  • Tremor, ataxia, weakness
  • Polyuria, polydipsia
  • Vomiting, diarrhea
  • Cognitive impairment

Chronic adverse effects:

  • Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
  • Thyroid dysfunction
  • Hyperparathyroidism

The most effective means of treating lithium toxicity is dialysis. It is necessary for severe poisoning cases, where:

  • The patient is exhibiting symptoms of toxicity, or
  • Lithium concentration is 4 mEq/L or more.

 Ebstein's anomaly: This is a rare congenital cyanotic heart disease caused by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. It is a teratogenic effect of lithium, a drug used for prophylaxis in manic disorder.

Lithium is thus avoided in the first trimester and during lactation. An antipsychotic like olanzapine should be considered instead of prophylactic management.

If lithium is to be continued, then:

  • The dose should be tapered to the lower end of the therapeutic range
  • It should be given in divided doses
  • The levels should be checked every two weeks
  • The woman should be hydrated well throughout labour
  • Withholding lithium therapy for 24-48 hours before delivery is recommended

choices.title: Vascular dementia
choices.correct_explanation:
Vascular dementia is a type of cognitive impairment caused by multiple small strokes or reduced blood flow to the brain, leading to rapid or stepwise cognitive decline. The progression often occurs within months and is accompanied by focal neurological signs.

Vascular Dementia

·         The criteria for the clinical diagnosis of vascular dementia include:

o   Cognitive decline from a previously higher level of functioning

o   Presence of focal signs on neurological examination, consistent with stroke

o   A relationship between the above two, based on the presence of one or more of the following:

§  Onset of dementia within 3 months following a recognized stroke

§  Abrupt deterioration in cognitive functions, or fluctuating, stepwise progression of cognitive deficits.

·         Imaging findings in vascular dementia include extensive leukoencephalopathy (white matter lesions), resulting from cerebral small-vessel disease or a variable number of infarcts in large-vessel territories.

Note:

·         Subcortical or small vessel dementia, can sometimes have an insidious onset.

·         In classic vascular dementia, since infarcts are accumulated in a stepwise fashion, deterioration is similarly abrupt and stepwise rather than smoothly gradual.

·         Population data suggest that the risk of developing dementia, both vascular and neurodegenerative, among people with diabetes followed for 20 years is roughly double that of those without diabetes.

Catastrophic dementia

·         This term is not a recognized medical diagnosis. It actually refers to a behavioral reaction, not a type of dementia.

·         “Catastrophic reaction” (often confused as “catastrophic dementia”) describes an emotional outburst — such as anger, crying, or panic — that occurs when a person with dementia becomes overwhelmed by frustration or failure during a task.

·         It is a symptom or response seen in dementia, not a separate disease process or cause of cognitive decline.

·         Example: A patient with Alzheimer’s disease starts crying uncontrollably and yelling when unable to button a shirt — this is a catastrophic reaction, not catastrophic dementia.

Mild Neurocognitive Disorder

·         Mild neurocognitive disorder or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a level of cognitive impairment which is:

  • Not severe enough to be diagnosed as dementia
  • Not mild enough to be called a part of the normal aging process.

·         General Criteria for Mild Cognitive Impairment:

  • Not normal, but does not meet criteria for dementia syndrome either.
  • Cognitive decline:

§  The patient and/or informant report an impairment in objective cognitive tasks.

§  Evidence of decline over time in objective cognitive tasks.

  • Preserved basic activities of daily living/minimal impairment in complex instrumental functions.
  • MMSE score between 25-27 (out of 30)
  • Single domain amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment usually progresses to Alzheimer's disease.

Borderline Personality Disorder       

  • Borderline personality disorder is classified under cluster B. It is characterized by an unstable affect, mood swings, marked impulsivity, unstable relationships, recurrent suicidal behavior, chronic feelings of emptiness or boredom, identity disturbance, and inappropriate anger. If stressed, the patient may become psychotic.
  • In borderline personality disorder the main defense mechanism such patients use is splitting i.e., distorting interpersonal relationships by considering each person to be either completely good or bad, with no middle ground.     
  • Micropsychotic episodes (short-lived psychotic episodes) are commonly seen in borderline personality disorder. These psychotic symptoms are almost always circumscribed, fleeting, or doubtful.
  • Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), a form of psychotherapy is the treatment of choice for borderline personality disorder and is effective, especially for those with parasuicidal behavior, such as frequent cutting.   

Bipolar disorders

Types of bipolar disorder: 

Bipolar I

Bipolar II

·         Episodes of mania with or without episodes of major depressive disorder (at least one-lifetime episode of mania is required for diagnosis).

·         The average age of onset of bipolar I disorder is 20 years, and in more than half of the cases, the onset is frequently in late adolescence.

·         The lifetime prevalence of bipolar type 1 disorder is 0 to 2.4%.

·         Bipolar type 1 disorder is seen with an equal prevalence among men and women (unlike depression, which has a higher prevalence among females than males).

·         Episodes of hypomania with episodes of major depressive disorder (negative history of a manic episode is required for diagnosis).

·         The lifetime prevalence of bipolar type 2 disorder is 0.3-4.8%.

 

 

  • The prevalence of bipolar disorder is higher in higher socio-economic strata. By contrast, schizophrenia has a higher prevalence in the lower socio-economic strata.
  • Suicide attempt is seen in approximately 15% of patients affected by bipolar disorder.

·         Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is used in the treatment of anxiety and panic disorders, depression, phobia, OCD, personality disorders and somatoform disorders.

·         Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is based on the psychological significance of the cognitive triad:

  • Individuals belief about themselves.
  • Their personal world (including the people in their lives).
  • Their future.

·         Problematic and biased interpretations related to this cognitive triad may lead to excessive emotional distress. 

·         CBT is applied to identify these faulty ideas and beliefs, make patients aware of the underlying assumptions that drive them, and modifying their responses to them.

·         The three components of cognitive therapy are:

  • Didactic aspects: Explaining to patients the cognitive triad, schemas, and faulty logic. The therapist must explain all the aspects of treatment.
  • Cognitive techniques: These involve four steps -

§  Eliciting automatic thoughts - Asking the patient about the thought that causes the emotional reaction in them.

§  Testing validity of the automatic thoughts.

§  Identifying the general maladaptive assumptions (a belief that is false and rationally unsupported).

§  Testing the validity of maladaptive assumptions.

choices.correct_explanation:
Acute hypotension is one of the most common complications during hemodialysis. It occurs primarily due to excessive fluid removal (ultrafiltration), leading to intravascular volume depletion and reduced venous return. The first and immediate nursing action is to stop ultrafiltration to prevent further fluid loss and position the patient supine with legs elevated (Trendelenburg-like position) to promote venous return and restore perfusion. Once the patient’s condition stabilizes, IV fluids (e.g., normal saline) may be given if ordered, and ultrafiltration settings can later be readjusted.

Key Nursing Actions on hemodialysis:

·         Stop ultrafiltration immediately.

·         Reposition the patient supine with legs elevated.

·         Check vital signs and notify the physician.

·         Administer IV fluids if ordered.

·         Review ultrafiltration settings before resuming dialysis. 

Other Options:

  • Option-a: Administer IV dopamine - Not the first-line intervention. Dopamine is reserved for persistent hypotension unresponsive to volume restoration and position changes.
  • Option-b: Slow the ultrafiltration and continue blood pressure monitoring - Partially correct but not sufficient when BP drops drastically (79/58 mmHg). Ultrafiltration should be stopped immediately, not just slowed.
  • Option-d: Administer IV fluids (normal saline/albumin) - Supportive measure after stopping ultrafiltration and positioning. Should be done as per physician’s order if hypotension persists.

choices.correct_explanation:
After an adrenalectomy, particularly for Cushing’s syndrome, the body’s cortisol levels fluctuate significantly. Cortisol directly affects glucose metabolism, so both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia may occur depending on postoperative cortisol replacement and adrenal recovery. Therefore, frequent blood glucose monitoring is the highest priority in the immediate postoperative period.  

Adrenalectomy   

·         Surgical removal of one or both adrenal glands.

·         Performed under general anesthesia using an open incision or laparoscopic approach.

·         Use:  

o   Indicated for adrenal cancer and benign hormone-secreting tumors such as aldosterone-producing adenoma, pheochromocytoma, or idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia causing severe Cushing’s syndrome.

o   Also considered for pituitary-dependent Cushing’s disease when transsphenoidal hypophysectomy is not feasible or contraindicated.  

·         Postoperative course:

o   Maintain continuous hemodynamic monitoring (CVP, BP, pulse, and occasionally pulmonary wedge pressure) to ensure fluid and electrolyte balance.

o   Administer saline–dextrose IV fluids as prescribed.

o   Provide IV cortisol replacement for 24–48 hours, then begin mineralocorticoid therapy on the 2nd postoperative day.

o   Bilateral adrenalectomy: Requires lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement.

o   Unilateral adrenalectomy: May need temporary cortisol therapy, tapered gradually over 6 months to 2 years as ACTH-adrenal function recovers.      

o   Usual hospital stay: 4–5 days for open surgery and 2–3 days for laparoscopic procedures.

o   No activity restrictions are generally required after laparoscopic adrenalectomy.

·         Complications: Adrenal crisis, hypo or hypertension, high or low blood glucose, fluid and electrolyte imbalance.   

·         Nursing Process Elements

o   Maintain invasive hemodynamic monitoring.

o   Check serum electrolytes daily and blood glucose every 4 hours.

o   Record intake and output hourly and monitor daily weight.

o   Observe for signs of inadequate glucocorticoid dosage such as weakness, anorexia, nausea, or vomiting.

o   Use strict aseptic technique during wound care and avoid infection exposure due to increased cortisol levels.

o   Alternate activity with rest to manage fatigue and activity intolerance.

o   Prevent orthostatic hypotension by assisting with position changes, slow movements, and using elastic stockings.

o   Support ambulation until blood pressure stabilizes.

choices.title: Increase oxygen flow rate further to maintain saturation above 98%
Reduce oxygen flow to maintain target SpO₂ between 88–92%
choices.correct_explanation:
In patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), the drive to breathe is often hypoxic (stimulated by low oxygen levels), rather than hypercapnic (high CO₂).
Providing excessive oxygen can suppress the hypoxic respiratory drive, leading to CO₂ retention (hypercapnia), respiratory acidosis, and respiratory failure. Therefore, the target oxygen saturation (SpO₂) for COPD patients on oxygen therapy is 88–92%, as recommended by GOLD and British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines.

Reading of a pulse oximetry showing 110% is technically impossible and indicates device error or artifact, but the clinical cue here is over-oxygenation, requiring reduction in flow rate.

Points to Remember            

                                                   

Key Nursing Actions: Patient on Oxygen therapy in COPD

·         Decreased oxygen in the blood is the stimulus for breathing in a patient with COPD. Therefore, if oxygen is administered there is the risk that respiratory arrest will occur because high oxygen saturation levels in the blood eliminate the stimulus for breathing.

·         This is a particular risk with the administration of 100% oxygen. The normal stimulus to breathe is an increase in CO2 in the blood but the patient with COPD has become insensitive to CO2 because of long-term elevated levels associated with the COPD.

·         Reassess oxygen flow and titrate to maintain SpO₂ between 88–92%.

·         Monitor arterial blood gases (ABGs) if available.

·         Observe for signs of CO₂ retention: Drowsiness, confusion, headache, and flushed skin.

·         Notify the physician if hypercapnia symptoms develop.    

 

    • Option-a: Increase oxygen flow rate further to maintain saturation above 98% - Increasing oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention and respiratory acidosis in COPD patients.   
    • Option-c: Stop oxygen immediately and keep the patient on room air - Dangerous — May cause hypoxemia, leading to tissue hypoxia and cardiac arrhythmias.

Option-d: Administer a sedative to reduce respiratory distress - Contraindicated — Sedatives depress respiratory drive and worsen hypercapnia.

choices.correct_explanation:
A spinal cord injury (SCI) below the T4 level affects the thoracic region, sparing the cervical spinal cord, which controls the neck, shoulders, and upper extremities. Hence, the expected presentation is paraplegia — loss of motor and sensory function in the lower extremities — while upper limb and respiratory muscle function remain intact.    

Neurological Correlation

Functional Loss

Description

C1–C4

Quadriplegia + respiratory paralysis

Loss of all limb movement and diaphragm function → requires ventilatory support

C5–C8

Quadriplegia

Varying loss of arm and hand movement depending on level

T1–T12

Paraplegia

Upper limbs intact; trunk and lower limb function affected below lesion

Below L1

Cauda equina involvement

Flaccid paralysis of lower limbs and bowel/bladder dysfunction

 

Since T4 is part of the upper thoracic segment, the arms and diaphragm (controlled by C3–C5 via phrenic nerve) remain functional.

Spinal Cord Injury 

·         Above C3 injuries are generally fatal.

·         Above C4 respiratory failure is common.

·         Complete transection of the cord—complete loss of sensory and motor function below level of injury.

·         Incomplete transection—some spinal cord tracts are intact so there is some sensory or motor function below the level of injury.

·         Tetraplegia (formerly quadriplegia)—loss of function in arms, legs, trunk, bowel, and bladder due to a cervical cord injury.

·         Quadriparesis—weakness of both upper and lower extremities.

·         Paraplegia—loss of function in legs, bowel, and bladder resulting from a thoracic, lumbar, or sacral cord injury. 

·         Paraparesis—weakness of lower extremities.

·         Level of injury—lowest neurologic segment with normal sensory and motor function.

Hyperflexion injury

·         Head and neck are forced into hyperflexion as in a head on motor vehicle accident   

·         Usually affects C5-C6

Hyperextension injury

·         Head and neck are forced back and downward as in rear end motor vehicle accidents and falls striking the chin

·         Middle to lower cervical spine most often affected

·         Damage is often major   

Compression injury

·         Results from extreme vertical force as in being hit on top of the head or forceful landing on the feet or buttocks  

·         Cervical and thoracolumbar spine most often affected

Rotational injury

·         Extreme lateral flexion or twisting of the head

Penetrating injury

 

·         Direct contact of an object such as a bullet or knife with the spinal cord

·         Low-impact (low-speed) injury results in damage, localized at site of impact; high-impact (high-speed) injury, as from of a gunshot, results in widespread damage.

 

Autonomic hyperreflexia (previously dysreflexia)

·         Emergency that can result in stroke, blindness, or death.

·         Over response of the sympathetic nervous system because below the injury it is shut off from inhibitory control of centers in the brain.        

·         Occurs with injuries at T6 or above after period of spinal shock is over.

·         Stimuli initiating the response include: bladder distention (most common cause), bowel distention, local pressure or irritation in groin, sacral or penile areas, tight clothing, urethral catheterization or digital or other stimulation of anus, abdominal or pelvic stimulation as from sexual activity, menses, UTI, cholecystitis, gastritis, cold, heat, and drafts.

·         Sympathetic stimulus from below area of injury causes vasoconstriction and paroxysmal hypertension; this in turn leads to bradycardia and vasodilation above level of injury in an unsuccessful attempt to lower BP.

·         Pounding headache, nausea, nasal stuffiness, and blurred vision often accompany the hypertension.

Below injury, skin is pale or mottled, cool and has goosebumps due to profound vasoconstriction; above injury, skin is flushed and diaphoretic due to the vasodilation.

choices.correct_explanation:
A platelet count of 18,000/µL (18 × 10³/µL) indicates severe thrombocytopenia, which poses a high risk of spontaneous bleeding, including intracranial, gastrointestinal, or mucosal hemorrhage. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate monitoring and intervention.

Chemotherapy      

·         Chemotherapy is used for the cure of cancer, long-term control of tumor growth, or for palliative shrinking of the tumor.

·         Adjuvant Therapy: Given with surgery or radiation to eliminate micrometastases.

·         Effectiveness: Drugs targeting dividing cells work best in small, rapidly growing tumors, while agents acting on non-dividing cells are useful in slow-growing tumors.

·         Combination Therapy: Preferred approach as it:  

o   Attacks cancer cells through multiple mechanisms,

o   Reduces risk of drug resistance, and

o   Minimizes toxicity by distributing side effects across different organs and time frames.

·         Drug Classes: Include alkylating agents, antimetabolites, plant alkaloids, antitumor antibiotics, and corticosteroids.   

·         Dosage Basis: Calculated using body surface area (BSA) derived from height and weight.

·         Routes of Administration: Oral, subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous (commonly via central venous access device), topical, or direct instillation into specific sites like the bladder, peritoneum, cerebrospinal fluid, or tumor bed.

·         Common Side Effects:     

o   Occur primarily in rapidly dividing tissues—bone marrow, GI mucosa, hair follicles, and germ cells.

o   Other effects include fatigue and drug-specific organ toxicities.

Practice Alert

Monitoring for IV infiltration during administration of vesicant drugs is critical. If infiltration occurs, immediate treatment with the appropriate antidote and the correct hot or cold compress should be initiated to minimize tissue damage.

Table: Side effects of chemotherapy  

Affected Tissue/Organ

Symptoms

Notes

Management

Bone-marrow suppression

Each drug has a particular time at which maximum suppression occurs—for many drugs it is 7–10 days after drug administration

·         Implement regimen to maintain skin and mucous membrane integrity

·         Avoid injections, rectal treatments, and other invasive procedures such as urinary catheterization

·         Avoid medications that mask pain and other signs of infection

·         Minimize exposure to sources of infection: Good hand washing by staff; restrict contact with persons with colds or other infection; avoid or thoroughly wash and cook fruits and vegetables; avoid obviously infected items such as litter boxes, and used tissues

·         Monitor WBC and neutrophil count and for signs of infection

·         Report stat fever over 101°F or other signs of infection

·         Obtain bacterial and fungal cultures of body fluids before giving antibiotics

·         Administer antibiotics and colony-stimulating factors as ordered

May be mild such as bruising or a nosebleed or major hemorrhage into brain or GI tract

·         Avoid drugs which increase bleeding (ASA and NSAIDs)

·         After venipuncture, apply pressure for 5 min to site

·         Monitor platelet count

·         Monitor for signs of bleeding

·         Administer platelet Tx as ordered for count below 10,000/mm3, for active bleeding or before invasive procedures

·         Use soft toothbrush; avoid flossing and dental procedures

·         Use only electric shaver

·         Avoid activities that present risk of trauma

Anemia

Signs of decreased tissue perfusion in any organ: fatigue, decreased endurance, headache, dizziness, tachycardia, and dyspnea

·         Administer EPO and/or Tx as ordered

·         Design energy-conserving plan with patient

GI tract

Stomatitis

Timing usually parallels bone marrow suppression, i.e., 7–10 days after treatment

·         Remove and clean dentures or brush teeth with soft brush after eating and at bedtime, then rinse with salt and water or a mouthwash containing 6% alcohol

·         Floss daily unless contraindicated

·         Do not wear dentures if they rub or are rough or if mouth is sore

·         Lubricate lips and avoid irritants such as alcohol or tobacco

·         Rinse every 2–4 hrs, increase fluid intake and use artificial saliva PRN for dry mouth

·         Avoid spicy or acidic foods and use topical anesthetics and systemic analgesics PRN for sore mouth

Nausea and vomiting

·         Typically peaks in first 12 hrs; may be followed by delayed nausea lasting 2–5 d

·         Anticipatory N and V may also occur

·         Administer antiemetics

·         Monitor fluid and electrolyte status

Constipation and diarrhea

May be directly caused by drug but can be exacerbated by altered diet, opioid use, etc.

 

Hair follicles

Alopecia

Amount of hair loss is dose and route-dependent; ranges from thinning of scalp hair to complete loss of all body hair; begins 2–3 weeks after start of

Rx; reversible with regrowth starting 1–2 months after Rx and taking up to a year

 

Ovaries/testes

Altered fertility: Amenorrhea in young and menopause in older females; decreased sperm production and sperm and semen abnormalities in men

Most common with alkylating agents; fertility can be recovered but length and time for recovery depends on the drug and the dose; younger women more likely to recover than older

 

Specific drug-related organ toxicities

---

---

Cryoprotectant drugs protect normal tissue and prevent some toxicities

Heart (cardiac cells)

EKG changes, heart failure over long term

Occurs with anthracycline agents

 

Lungs

Pulmonary fibrosis

Occurs with bleomycin

 

Liver

Hepatic toxicity

Occurs with high doses of many drugs

 

Kidney

Nephrotoxicity

Occurs with cisplatin and high dose of methotrexate

Occurs with cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide

 

 

Assessment Alert

Neutropenic patients do not exhibit a normal inflammatory response. Mild localized tenderness and fever over 101°F may be the only signs of severe infection and represent a medical emergency.

choices.title: Slow IV infusion over 2–5 minutes with cardiac monitoring
choices.correct_explanation:
Calcium gluconate is given in severe hyperkalemia to stabilize the cardiac membrane — it does not lower serum potassium, but reduces the risk of fatal arrhythmias (like ventricular fibrillation or asystole).

Key Administration Guidelines:   

·         Route: Intravenous (IV) only.

·         Rate: Administer slowly over 2–5 minutes to prevent bradycardia or cardiac arrest.

·         Monitoring: Continuous ECG monitoring is mandatory during and after administration.

·         Dose: Typically, 10% calcium gluconate, 10 mL IV over 2–5 min.

·         Do not give IM or subcutaneous — causes tissue necrosis.

·         Do not give oral form for emergencies — absorption is slow and ineffective in acute settings.

Hyperkalemia (serum K+ > 5.5 mEq/L) 

·         Hyperkalemia develops when there is too much potassium in the body due to inadequate excretion by the kidney or malfunctioning of the distal tubule or decreased renal blood flow with insufficient sodium to be exchanged for potassium or excessive intake or movement of potassium out of cells into ECF.

Etiology:  

·         Renal failure

·         Medications such as tetracycline, antineoplastics, heparin, isoniazid, lithium, and potassium-conserving diuretics 

·         Acidosis

·         Insulin deficiency  

·         Adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease)

·         High oral or IV intake

·         Cell destruction: Burns, trauma, and malnutrition

Sign and Symptoms:  

·         Weakness, paresthesias of face, tongue, feet and hands; flaccid muscle paralysis, hyperactive DTRs, nausea, confusion.

·         ECG changes: Tall, peaked T waves, wide QRS intervals, prolonged PR intervals, bradycardia, cardiac dysrhythmias, heart block, and cardiac arrest with K+ greater than 7.0.

Dx: Measurement of serum K+.

Key Points     

Incorrect handling of blood samples can result in hemolysis of blood cells with release of intracellular potassium thereby giving a false, high serum K+ measurement.

 

Rx:   

·         Varies with degree of hyperkalemia

·         Restrict K+— no supplements, no transfusions of whole blood products

·         IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinate plasma causing a shift of K+ into the cells

·         Kayexalate (oral or rectal) to remove K+

·         Dialysis to remove K+

·         Treat underlying cause

Clinical Alert

Emergency management of hypokalemic cardiac effects: IV calcium gluconate antagonizes effect of K+ on the heart

Nursing Process Elements

·         Stop any infusions containing potassium and withhold potassium supplements.

·         Monitor for neuromuscular sign and symptoms.

·         Monitor cardiac function.

·         Restrict potassium intake: Avoid administering potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, high-potassium foods, and use of salt substitutes all of which are high in potassium.

choices.correct_explanation:
• Before starting antibiotic therapy, the nurse must collect culture specimens (such as blood, urine, sputum, or wound culture) to identify the causative organism and ensure that the prescribed antibiotic is appropriate. Administering antibiotics before obtaining cultures can alter bacterial growth and lead to inaccurate culture results, making it difficult to determine the right treatment.
  • Option-a: Administer antibiotics immediately — antibiotics should not be started until cultures are obtained, unless it’s a life-threatening emergency like septic shock.  
  • Option-b: Give antipyretic before starting antibiotics — fever control is secondary to identifying and treating the cause of infection.
  • Option-d: Start IV fluids and observe the patient’s Response - Supportive care may be needed but not the first priority before cultures and antibiotics.
  • Clinical Tip: Always follow the “culture first, then antibiotic” principle — unless immediate antibiotic therapy is lifesaving.

choices.title: Hemorrhage
choices.correct_explanation:
After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG), close monitoring of mediastinal (chest tube) drainage is essential to detect postoperative bleeding or tamponade early.

Normal postoperative drainage:

·         Up to 100–150 mL/hr during the first few hours is expected.

·         >200 mL/hr for 2–3 consecutive hours or sudden increase in drainage with hypotension indicates active bleeding (hemorrhage) and may require urgent re-exploration.

In this case:

·         Drainage = 250 mL/hr × 3 hours = 750 mL in 3 hours,

·         Associated hypotension, strongly suggests postoperative hemorrhage.

Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG)

·         A blood vessel from another part of the body is used to bypass the obstructed coronary artery. Attachment is made from the aorta or if using the internal mammary artery, the proximal end remains attached to the subclavian artery, and the other end of the vessel is attached to the distal portion of the obstructed coronary artery thus, providing revascularization of the heart.

·         CABG is performed on a stopped heart and requires the use of extracorporeal circulation by the cardiopulmonary bypass pump.

·         Uses: For clients with severe CAD, clients with blockages greater than 70% of two or three coronary arteries, left main coronary artery lesions greater than 60%, unstable angina, angina which cannot be controlled by medical therapy or when complications have developed from percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

Point to Remember:

When using cardiopulmonary bypass pump, the patient receives Heparin to prevent thrombus formation and hypothermia is maintained to decrease the body’s metabolic needs.

·         Preparation: Usual preoperative care for patient undergoing open heart surgery including physical, emotional, and psychosocial assessment; provide emotional support; patient education concerning the anatomy and physiology of the heart and the surgical procedure, postoperative procedures and equipment including hemodynamic monitoring equipment, ventilator, endotracheal tube, pacing wires, chest tubes, and nasogastric tube, ICU policies and visiting hours, possible complications and treatments, pain management, and sensory stimuli and sensory overload.

·         Postoperative course: As for clients undergoing open heart surgery, patient will be in an intensive care unit for 1–2 days and will be discharged home after a total hospital stay of 5–7 days

·         Nursing Process Elements

o   Monitor hemodynamic measures.

o   Assess cardiac monitoring.

o   Assess peripheral pulses.

o   Assess bowel sounds and measure abdominal girth every 8 hours.

o   Measure and record I and O hourly including chest tube and NG drainage.

o   Monitor laboratory values especially Hct and Hgb, ABGs, CBC, APPT, and electrolytes.

o   Keep temporary pacemaker at bedside.

o   Monitor core body temperature and keep temperature above 96.8°F (36°C).

o   Assess pain level.  

o   Administer medications as ordered.

o   Note ETT placement and ventilator settings.

o   Provide emotional support to client and family.

o   Evaluate respiratory status. 

o   Assess incisions for presence of infection and drainage.

o   Turn and have client deep breath.

o   Assess for symptoms and signs of complications including thrombophlebitis, pulmonary embolism, CHF, and cardiac tamponade.   

Other options:      

·         Option-a: Cardiac tamponade - In tamponade, drainage decreases or stops suddenly due to clot obstruction of the tube, with rising central venous pressure (CVP), muffled heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus — not continuous high output.     

·         Option-c: Pulmonary embolism - Causes sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, and hypoxemia, not high chest tube output.

Option-d: Pleural effusion - Develops gradually and produces dyspnea and dullness on percussion, not acute high-volume bloody drainage.

In a postoperative patient (2 days after cholecystectomy) who develops fever and leukocytosis (WBC = 18,000/mm³), infection is the most likely cause — possibly due to wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess, or line sepsis.

Before starting empirical antibiotics, it is essential to identify the causative organism by collecting appropriate cultures. This ensures accurate diagnosis and guides antibiotic selection.

Cholecystectomy

·         Cholecystectomy is the removal of gall bladder; most done laparoscopically, open done if acute inflammation or adhesions are present; T tube is placed into common bile duct if duct is explored.

·         Use: Treat cholelithiasis and cholecystitis.

·         Preparation: Food and fluid restriction, cleansing enemas, NG tube and urinary catheter before laparoscopic procedures to decompress stomach and bladder and decrease the risk of accidental perforation.  

Point to Remember:   

             Check PT of patients with obstructive jaundice. Vitamin K may be needed before surgery.

·         Postoperative course: Laparoscopic - minimal pain

§  Serosanguinous drainage with small amount of bile expected from Penrose drain in first 24 hours; drain removed in 48 hours

§  T-tube drainage of 500 mL in first 24 hours, decreasing to about 200 mL/24 hours for next 3–4 days; initially bloody then green–brown

§  Diet progressed as tolerated, dietary fat may be limited temporarily

§  Excess bile drainage may be returned to client via NG tube to prevent electrolyte imbalance or synthetic bile salts given

§  Position in left Sims’ for comfort.

choices.correct_explanation:
Red tag (Immediate) — Assigned to patients with life-threatening but treatable conditions who can be saved with immediate medical intervention.

·         The patient with pinpoint pupils, bronchospasm, and frothy salivation likely has organophosphate poisoning (a cholinergic crisis) due to chemical exposure in the explosion.

Option-d: Patient in cardiac arrest with no pulse- Black tag (Deceased/Expectant) — No pulse means no chance of survival in triage scenarios; resources are not used for resuscitation.

Option-d:  Patient with minor abrasions and stable condition - Green tag (Minor) — Can wait for treatment after critical cases are managed.

choices.correct_explanation:
Conscious sedation, also known as moderate sedation, is a drug-induced depression of consciousness during which the patient: 

·         Remains responsive to verbal commands or light tactile stimulation,

·         Maintains protective airway reflexes,

·         Has adequate spontaneous ventilation, and

·         Experiences reduced anxiety and discomfort.

It is commonly used in minor procedures such as endoscopy, cardiac catheterization, or wound debridement, where full anesthesia is not required.

Conscious Sedation

·         Definition: A controlled, minimally depressed level of consciousness in which the patient can maintain airway reflexes, respond to verbal or tactile stimuli, and tolerate uncomfortable procedures with minimal distress.

·         Drugs Used: Usually achieved with short-acting benzodiazepines (e.g., midazolam) and/or opioids (e.g., fentanyl).

o   Reversal agents: Naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines.

·         Indications:  

o   Short diagnostic or therapeutic procedures – biopsy, endoscopy, bone marrow aspiration, radiologic or radiation procedures, painful dressing changes.

o   Adjunct to local/regional anesthesia for dental, suturing, or minor surgical procedures.

·         Preparation:

  • Prolonged labour

o   Delivery

·        Timing:

§  Routine postpartum administration of anti-D immune globulin to at-risk pregnancies within 72 hours of delivery decreases the alloimmunization rate by 90 percent.       

§  Should be given only if the baby born is Rh +ve and Direct Coombs Test done on baby’s blood is negative.

§  Additionally, the provision of Anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks of gestation (Non-immunized Rh-negative primigravida) reduces the third-trimester alloimmunization rate from approximately 2 percent to 0.1 percent.  

·        Dose:

o   Ideally, the amount of Anti D should be calculated according to the volume of fetomaternal bleed by doing a Kleihauer test.

o   All Rh-negative unsensitized women should receive 50 µg of Rh-immune globulin IM in the first trimester (Gestational age < 12 weeks) in the following conditions:

§  Within 72 hours of induced or spontaneous abortion

§  Ectopic/molar pregnancy

§  Chorionic villus sampling

  • Women with a pregnancy beyond 12 weeks should receive a full dose of 300 µg. Generally, a 300 µg dose will protect a woman from fetal hemorrhage of up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood (i.e., approximately 15 mL of fetal cell).
  • The dose in the 3rd trimester and post-delivery is 300 µg or 1500 international units (IU).

·        Calculation of dose:    

  • Volume of fetal blood entering maternal circulation is estimated by Kleihauer-Betke test.
  • If the volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage is greater than 30 mL whole blood, the dose of Rh-immune globulin calculated is 10 µg for every 0.5 mL of fetal RBCs.
  • The calculation is done as follows:

§  300 micrograms of Anti-D can neutralize 15 mL of fetal RBCs or 30 mL of fetal whole blood.

§  50 micrograms of Anti-D can neutralize 2.5 mL of fetal RBCs.

  • If there are 80 fetal RBCs in 50 LPF in maternal peripheral blood film, it represents transplacental hemorrhage to the extent of 4 mL of fetal blood.

·         A non-invasive test that evaluates fetal wellbeing by monitoring the fetal heart rate in response to fetal movements over a 20-minute period using a cardiotocograph (CTG). A reactive NST indicates a healthy fetus, while a non-reactive NST may raise concerns about fetal distress.

·         During an NST, the mother is placed in a comfortable position, and external monitors are attached to her abdomen to record the fetal heart rate and any fetal movements for 20-30 minutes.

·         Interpretation of NST:      

o   Reactive

§  Reassure the patient and send back home  

o   Non-reactive - biophysical profile (BPP) has to be assessed.

·         A reactive NST (presence of accelerations in fetal heart rate with movements) indicates good fetal health, while a non-reactive NST (lack of sufficient accelerations) may necessitate further testing or intervention.

choices.title: Aggressive IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics
choices.correct_explanation:
This woman presents 10 days’ post–induced abortion with: Fever, abdominal pain and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. These are classic signs of septic abortion — a life-threatening infection of the uterus and surrounding tissues following abortion.

The first and most urgent step is to: Stabilize the patient — address shock and infection. Hence, aggressive IV fluids for volume resuscitation and treatment of possible septic shock and simultaneously broad-spectrum IV antibiotics to control infection and cover likely pathogens (aerobes + anaerobes) are done.

Clinical features of septic abortion:

·         Fever with chills and rigors

·         Abdominal or chest pain

·         Diarrhea and vomiting

·         Renal angle tenderness

·         Offensive purulent vaginal discharge

Clinical grading of septic abortion:

·         Grade I - Infection localized in the uterus

·         Grade Il - Infection spreads to parametrium, tubes, ovaries, or pelvic peritoneum

·         Grade Ill - Generalized peritonitis, endotoxic shock, jaundice, or acute renal failure

Management 

Empirical antibiotic therapy in septic abortion is started for the broadest microbial coverage. Piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem and clindamycin are given intravenously. Antibiotics can be changed once culture sensitivity reports are available. 

 Organisms causing toxic shock syndrome in septic abortion:

·         Streptococcus pyogenes

·         Clostridium perfringens

·         Clostridium sordellii

The given case scenario is suggestive of an imperforate hymen, which has led to cryptomenorrhea. This is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract.

·         The menstrual fluid gets collected in the reproductive tract. When this collection occurs in the vagina, it is known as hematocolpos. If the collection extends to the uterus, it is known as hematometra. The collection of blood in the fallopian tubes is called hematosalpinx.

o   Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen.

o   Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen.

·         Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis.

·         Management:

o   Imperforate hymen - A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function.

o   Transverse vaginal septum - Extensive dissection and vaginoplasty is required.

• The cardiac monitor in the image shows a very rapid, regular, narrow QRS complex tachycardia with a heart rate of around 185 beats per minute, which is typical for Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) in a child.  
  • In pediatric SVT, the impulse originates above the ventricles (usually from the atria or AV node) and causes a regular, narrow complex rhythm. The P waves are often absent or buried in the preceding T waves because of the fast rate. The child’s blood pressure (49/35 mmHg) also indicates hemodynamic instability, which can occur due to poor ventricular filling at such a high rate.

Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)   

Key features:   

·         Rapid, regular narrow-complex tachycardia

·         Rate >180 bpm in children  

·         P waves absent or merged with T waves  

·         Often associated with low blood pressure and poor perfusion

Other Options:

  • Option-c: Atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular rate – AF shows an irregularly irregular rhythm without distinct P waves, which is not seen here. The rhythm here is regular.    

Option-d: Sinus tachycardia – Although sinus tachycardia can occur in children, the rate rarely exceeds 180 bpm in younger children and is usually accompanied by visible P waves before each QRS complex.

Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac
Gastric lavage is contraindicated in kerosene poisoning
choices.correct_explanation:
·         Kerosene is a hydrocarbon, and its major toxicity is due to aspiration into the lungs, leading to chemical pneumonitis rather than systemic absorption. When a child ingests kerosene, the primary concern is preventing aspiration. Any procedure that increases the risk of vomiting — such as gastric lavage, induction of emesis, or insertion of a nasogastric/orogastric tube — can worsen the situation by causing kerosene to enter the respiratory tract.    

·         Therefore, gastric lavage is contraindicated in kerosene ingestion, as it increases the risk of aspiration and respiratory complications. The correct management involves:

o   Keeping the airway clear,   

o   Monitoring for respiratory distress, and

o   Providing supportive care, including oxygen and bronchodilators if necessary.

·         Activated charcoal and lavage are both not useful, since kerosene is poorly adsorbed and lavage carries significant risk.

 

Other Options:    

·         Option-a: Perform gastric lavage with a large-bore (32 Fr) tube – Gastric lavage can cause vomiting and aspiration, leading to chemical pneumonitis; hence, it is contraindicated.

·         Option-b: Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac – Inducing vomiting increases the risk of aspiration of kerosene into the lungs, which can cause severe respiratory distress.

·         Option-d: Insert orogastric tube for continuous aspiration – Insertion of a tube into the stomach also carries a high risk of aspiration and does not provide any benefit in kerosene poisoning.

General Lines of Treatment of Poisoning

·         Decontamination: Emesis, gastric lavage, catharsis, activated charcoal, and whole bowel irrigation

Gastric Lavage - Most Important Topic    

·         Gastric lavage is very effective within 1 hour of poison ingestion.

·         Patient in left lateral position or sitting position.

·         Tubes used for gastric lavage: Lavacuator (Best), Ewald's tube, Boas tube, Ryles tube.

·         Complication of gastric lavage: Perforation, hemorrhage, aspiration, and laryngeal spasm.

·         Contraindications: Comatose patients, corrosive (except phenol), esophageal varices, volatile poisons, convulsant poisons.

Composition of Universal Antidote

·         Charcoal (2 parts) + Magnesium oxide (1 part) + Tannic acid (1 part)

·         Mechanism   

o   Charcoal - Absorbs poisons;

o   Magnesium oxide - Neutralizes acids;

Activated Charcoal

choices.correct_explanation:
• After a tonsillectomy, one of the most serious postoperative complications is hemorrhage from the surgical site. Bleeding may not always be visible because the child often swallows the blood instead of spitting it out. Therefore, frequent swallowing — especially when the child is resting or sleeping — is an early and important sign of bleeding in the throat. Early recognition is crucial to prevent airway obstruction or aspiration of blood.
  • Option-b: Elevation of blood pressure - Increased blood pressure may occur later as a response to blood loss or distress, but it is not an early indicator of bleeding.
  • Option-c: Sudden onset of hoarseness – Hoarseness may occur due to laryngeal edema or trauma during surgery, not necessarily from bleeding. It is not a specific sign of hemorrhage.
  • Option-d: Increased throat discomfort – Some degree of throat pain or discomfort is expected after tonsillectomy and is not specific to bleeding. It does not reliably indicate early hemorrhage.         

Tonsillectomy

·         Tonsillectomy is the removal of the palatine tonsils; bleeding areas are cauterized and sutured; it can be combined with an adenoidectomy—removal of the adenoids; most common surgery for children. 

·         Use: Tonsillectomy treats recurrent tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, hypertrophy of tonsils causing swallowing difficulty, difficult breathing; adenoidectomy relieves persistent otitis media, breathing and swallowing difficulty, sleep apnea, and speech distortion.  

·         Preparation: NPO, IV, check temperature; child needs to be without a fever and without a sore throat; no respiratory infection for about 2 weeks before surgery; no aspirin or ibuprofen for 2 weeks before surgery; assess for loose teeth; ask if child has been given herbal medication.

Postoperative course:     

·         Monitor vital sign frequently, also for airway obstruction, and respiratory distress.

·         Check for signs of hemorrhage: Increased pulse, low BP, restlessness, and frequent swallowing.

·         Begin diet with ice chips and, flavored ice pops but nothing brown or red which may cause emesis to look like old or new blood.    

  • Low-grade fever and earache are common postoperative symptoms.

choices.title: Failure of kidney to concentrate urine
choices.correct_explanation:
• The child has been kept nothing by mouth (NPO) for 6–8 hours, which can cause mild dehydration and an increase in serum sodium levels (hypernatremia). Normally, in response to rising serum sodium, the pituitary gland releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which acts on the renal tubules to conserve water and produce concentrated urine.        
  • However, in this case, despite the elevated serum sodium (150 mEq/L), the child is passing dilute urine, indicating that the kidneys are not responding appropriately to ADH or failing to concentrate urine. This situation suggests a defect either in ADH secretion (central diabetes insipidus) or in the renal tubular response to ADH (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus). Therefore, the most likely reason is failure of the kidney to concentrate urine.
  • Option-a: Increased extracellular fluid volume – Increased ECF volume would lead to decreased ADH secretion and possibly dilute urine, but the patient is NPO and more likely dehydrated, not fluid overloaded.   
  • Option-c: Increased antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion – If ADH secretion were increased, the urine would be concentrated, not dilute. 
  • Option-d: Excessive renal tubular reabsorption of water – Increased water reabsorption would lower serum sodium and produce concentrated urine, which is the opposite of the findings here.

choices.title: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome)
choices.correct_explanation:
The features of hematuria, oliguria, facial edema present with a history of skin infection points towards the diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

Management of Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

·         Supportive conservative therapy is the best step in the management of PSGN.

·         Management of PSGN is directed at treating the acute effects of renal insufficiency (sodium restriction and prescribing diuretics - usually with intravenous furosemide) and hypertension.

·         Although a 10-day course of systemic antibiotic therapy with penicillin is recommended to limit the spread of the nephritogenic organisms, antibiotic therapy does not affect the natural history of acute PSGN.     

·         Steroids and cyclosporine are not used in the management of PSGN.

Note:  In IgA nephropathy gross hematuria often occurs within 1-2 days of onset of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. In contrast, a longer latency period of about 1-2 weeks is observed in acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis.

Other options:    

IgA nephropathy 

·         Mesangial cell disease due to immune complex deposition.

·         IgA nephropathy presents more commonly as an acute nephritic syndrome or with asymptomatic hematuria. It presents with nephrotic syndrome quite rarely.

Nephrotic syndrome       

·         Hematuria is not a usual feature of nephrotic syndrome. It is a feature of nephritic syndrome. However, occasionally it is seen in the FSGS variant of nephrotic syndrome as well.

·         The commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is minimal change disease. (85% of cases).

·         Classic features of nephrotic syndrome:  

o   Nephrotic range proteinuria (>40mg/m2/hr urine protein: creatinine ratio >2)

o   Hypoalbuminemia (<2.5 g/dL)

o   Edema

o   Hyperlipidemia (cholesterol > 200 mg/dL)

o   Hypercoagulability

·         The glomeruli appear almost normal on microscopy, hence the name. Immunofluorescence microscopy are negative, and electron microscopy shows effacement of the epithelial cell foot processes.

·         Treatment: Steroids; 95% of patients respond.  

Minimal change disease  

·         Epithelial cell disease due to flattening of podocytes.

·         Minimal change nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome.

·         It is seen in ages 2-6 years with a clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome, that is, heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia.  

·         They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral edema. Renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome.

·         The diagnosis is confirmed by performing a urinalysis and urine protein: creatinine ratio. Nephrotic range proteinuria is proteinuria greater than 3.5 g per 24 hours (3+ or 4+) or a urine protein: creatinine ratio exceeding 2.

·         They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 2 mg/kg (max 60 mg) for 6 weeks followed by an alternate dose of 1.5 mg/kg (max 40 mg) for the next 6-8 weeks is recommended.

·         Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are as follows:

o   Cyclophosphamide

o   Calcineurin inhibitors: Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus

o   Mycophenolate    

o   Levamisole

o   Rituximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20)

Definitions regarding the course of nephrotic syndrome:

·         Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome: ≥2 relapses in 6 months or 3 or more relapses in 12 months.

·         Steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome: Relapse during steroid tapering or within 2 weeks of discontinuation.

·         Steroid resistance: Failure to achieve remission despite therapy with daily prednisolone for 6 weeks

Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors: cyclosporine and tacrolimus, mycophenolate, levamisole, and rituximab (a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20).

choices.correct_explanation:
·         Urine may be obtained by suprapubic bladder aspiration or urethral catheterization in children below 2 years. A colony count of >103/mL on suprapubic aspiration and >104/mL on urethral catheterization are considered significant.

Urinary tract infection (UTI)   

·         During infancy, UTIs are equally common in boys and girls because the route of infection is often hematogenous and boys have a higher incidence of urinary tract anomalies.  Beyond infancy, the incidence is higher in girls.

Microbiology    

Urinary tract infections in children are most commonly caused by the following:

·         Escherichia coli (Most common)

·         Klebsiella species

·         Proteus species

·         Staphylococcus saprophyticus

·         Enterococcus

·         Adenovirus and other viral infections (cause cystitis and gross hematuria)

Predisposing Factors

·         Recurrent UTIs are observed in 30-50% children, usually within 3 months of the first episode.

·         Predisposing factors for recurrent UTI are female sex, age below 6 months, bladder bowel dysfunction (BBD), VUR, obstructive uropathy, and repeated catheterization.

Clinical Features  

·         Neonates show features of sepsis with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, poor weight gain and lethargy.

·         Older infants have unexplained fever, frequent micturition and occasionally, seizures.

·         The presence of crying or straining during voiding, dribbling, weak or abnormal urine stream and palpable bladder suggest urinary obstruction.

·         The distinction is not necessary, since most UTI in children below 5 years of age involve the upper tracts.

·         Patients with high fever (>39°C), systemic toxicity, persistent vomiting, dehydration, renal angle tenderness or raised creatinine are considered as complicated. Patients with low grade fever, dysuria, frequency and urgency and absence of symptoms of complicated UTI are considered to have simple UTI. This distinction is important for purposes of therapy.

Clinical Pearls

It is difficult to distinguish between infection localized to the bladder (cystitis) and upper tracts (pyelonephritis).

Diagnosis

·         Significant bacteriuria is a colony count of >105/mL of a single species in a clean catch sample. A lower threshold (e.g. 104 colonies per mL) is applied in young infants with unexplained fever, particularly in presence of leukocyturia.       

·         Urine may be obtained by suprapubic bladder aspiration or urethral catheterization in children below 2 years. A colony count of >103/mL on suprapubic aspiration and >104/mL on urethral catheterization are considered significant.

·         Bag or diaper specimens should not be used for culture. The occurrence of significant bacteriuria in absence of symptoms is termed asymptomatic bacteriuria (Option-C).

·         The presence of >10 leukocytes per mm3 in fresh uncentrifuged sample, or >5 leukocytes per high power field in centrifuged sample is useful for screening. 

Imaging Studies  

·         In a child presenting with an episode of urinary tract infection (UTI), initial imaging should be ultrasonography of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder.

·         A voiding cystourethrogram is indicated only if the ultrasound study is abnormal, the patient has atypical features or after a recurrent febrile UTI.

·         Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scan may be done after 4-6 months of acute infection as it may help to locate and delineate the scarring.     

Treatment            

·         Infants below 3 months of age, and those with severe acute illness should initially receive parenteral antibiotics. Following initial IV antibiotic therapy, oral antibiotics usually suffice.

·         In all other patients, oral therapy with cefixime or coamoxiclav is started empirically.

·         Patients with cystitis can be managed with short course (3-5 days) of oral antibiotics; all others should receive therapy for 7-10 days.  

Ref: GHAI’s Essential Pediatrics; 10th Ed; Page No- 508

  • The heart rate remains below 60 beats/minute despite:

Preparation

  • Take 0.5 mg adrenaline
  • Add 9.5 mL normal saline
  • Final volume = 10 mL

choices.correct_explanation:
• The commonly available adrenaline ampoule is 1:1000, which contains:

1 mg adrenaline in 1 mL (i.e., 1 mg/mL).

  • In newborn resuscitation, adrenaline must be given intravenously only in 1:10,000 dilution, which means:

1 mg adrenaline in 10 mL (i.e., 0.1 mg/mL).

How to prepare 1:10,000 from the ampoule

  1. Draw entire 1 mL from the ampoule (1 mg adrenaline).
  2. Add 9 mL normal saline.
  3. Total volume becomes 10 mL.
  4. Final concentration becomes:

1 mg / 10 mL = 0.1 mg/mL = 1:10,000

That exact preparation is written in Option C.

Dose Point (Very Important)

  • Dose: 0.1 of 1:10,000 = 10 micrograms/kg (0.01 mg/kg)
  • The standard IV dose is then administered at 0.1 to 0.2 mL/kg (equivalent to 0.01–0.02 mg/kg).
  • Route: Umbilical vein (UVC)

Why other options are wrong

  • Option A: Gives 0.5 mg in 10 mL = 0.05 mg/mL, which is not 1:10,000.
  • Option B: Not a standard preparation and does not ensure correct concentration.
  • Option D: Gives 0.05 mg in 5 mL = 0.01 mg/mL, which is too dilute and incorrect.

Final Takeaway: Ampoule = 1 mg/1 mL (1:1000) → add 9 mL NS → 1 mg/10 mL (1:10,000). Hence option C.
